first_paragraph: São Paulo (EFE).- Supporters of Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva protested outside the São Paulo headquarters of tech giant Meta on Monday, six days before the election. They accused the company of favoring content from opposition candidate Flávio Bolsonaro.Organized by the platform «Não Se Meta,» the protest drew about 200 demonstrators who demanded that the company, led by Mark Zuckerberg, explain its actions. The protesters accused Meta of «interfering in the elections and harming President Lula by reducing the reach of his posts and boosting those of Flavio.»«Meta cannot be an invisible judge of the electoral process,» they argued outside the company’s Brazil headquarters, accusing it of committing electoral crimes since the 2018 election, when Jair Bolsonaro (2019-2023) became president.On Monday, the Superior Electoral Court gave Meta, the company that owns Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, 24 hours to demonstrate that it guarantees equal treatment for the campaigns

title: MiniMax M3.1 Flash (minimax.io)

title: I built a drone with only one motor [video] (youtube.com)
comments: Just want to mention that hobbyists into fixed wing RC aerobatics have been doing crazy stuff with variable pitch propellers (VPP) for several years. RC motors with integrated variable pitch propellers exist in small sizes, so no need to DIY the propeller for that application. Here's an example of the 4D aerobatics they enable: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j5EsvZNvVRs.This is similar to but different than what the creator of the one motor drone is doing since he's spinning at higher RPM with the pitch varying  under CPU control much faster than fixed wing aerobatic pilots who are controlling everything manually with insane skill. Yes, you should be (besides the flying skills), and yes, it is a hard technical problem.Normally the plane would use control surfaces, this one uses thrust vectoring with only one item providing thrust. Underactuated robotics are so cool. In the hobby BattleBots community, there is a design where the whole robot only has a single motor, but it's able to move in any direction and damage the opponent, all just by controlling the single motor's speed.Most robots have at least three motors, two drive sides and a weapon motor. The trick to getting away with one is integrating an impactor into the chassis of your bot, using the single wheel to spin up to ~3k RPM, then by tracking the rotation angle of the bot as it spins, you speed up a little while the wheel is pointing where you want to go, and slow it down a little when it's pointing the other direction.reply

https://underactuated.csail.mit.edu/

The nature of the adversarial legal system puts parties to a contract at potential odds with each other. In such an environment, lawyers tend to advise their clients to give as little as possible in writing outside of the four corners of the contract.In other words, finding out your rights is your job. That’s why you should hire your own counsel if you think you’ve been wronged. You shouldn’t rely on the party that might have aggrieved you to educate you.Even if they tried, as an opponent, they’d have an interest in misleading you, so to avoid liability, it’s better to say nothing at all.reply

title: It's still ok to enjoy programming (chriskiehl.com)
comments: Even if work is not life, hobby programming also has been affected.I worked hard a couple of years ago to reverse engineer a game to produce a very specific tool. Recently, the game was updated, so I worked on my free time to do a free contribution to the community, and then, a few hours later a tool that does the same thing appeared entirely vibecoded.Even if some parts of the community care about how a tool was made – Most don't, they just want something that fulfill the goal.Now even my hobby programming was overtaken by AI, something I did for love and expected no pay out of it whatsoever, which is... depressing, to say the least.reply

I tried to look at it like cooking, or baking: I can make damn good croissants. They'll never be quite as good as someone with a dough sheeter and handmade cultured butter, but my friends and family would never complain.The problem is, baking something and sharing it with others brings people together, there's smalltalk, catching up, other human stuff. Which in the end is kinda the point of it.Like your post says, with programming, it's mostly just a race to what achieves the goal, with the exception of demoscene and retro programming, I guess. I started learning ARM assembly so I could make a lisp implementation in it. It will be useless, no one will use it, and an AI could bang one out in a few minutes, but  overcoming that struggle to understand things in different ways has to be the goal with hobby programmers like myself, I guess.reply

> The problem is, baking something and sharing it with others brings people together ...Honestly, I don't see how this is a problem.> Which in the end is kinda the point of it.Absolutely.> Like your post says, with programming, it's mostly just a race to what achieves the goal ...Unless the joy of whatever programming one does is found in the path taken.> I started learning ARM assembly so I could make a lisp implementation in it. It will be useless, no one will use it, and an AI could bang one out in a few minutes ...Who cares if anyone uses it or if some other tooling could replicate what you choose to do if, in doing so, you enjoy it.Much like the "damn good croissants" you make, it doesn't matter what others could make. You make damn good croissants.Your happiness is yours.  Enjoy the path you take to find it.reply
They’re saying the problem is that programming doesn’t result in bringing people together. The problem is that the value of baking is not easily recreated in all hobbies.reply

Like chess, basketball, book clubs, board games, video games, popdarts, etc.reply

Yes, my favourite programming project is a tetris clone my family and one or two friends have played.The community you share with doesn't need to be online - your croissants aren't going out for delivery but I'm sure your friends and family appreciate them (and you). It can be the same with your software products, if you choose.reply

Well with programming there can be a creative aspect which is more like sharing art/music online... But unfortunately that's still affected. I've been putting out what I think are pretty banger projects, with a good level of polish, but it's like nobody cares anymore. Social media is saturated.reply

Yes, besides AI upending everything, it's been a long slow decline with internet communities in general for over a decade now. Instead of having to look for what we think is interesting and talking to people about it, an algorithm just decides what we're going to enjoyreply

I'd ask - is your hobby programming the tool, or distributing a tool you built for others to enjoy and working with that community?I'd say the post deals _strictly_ with the former. LLM code generation absolutely changes community dynamics, what other projects are published, etc.reply

Part of various communities is _doing_ something of shared interest together and accomplishing something as a group. Sometimes that group is trying to solve a novel problem or push the state of the art forward. When there is no need for a community to serve that purpose, it becomes a group of people who may not otherwise gel. It’s great when it works out otherwise, but I’ve enjoyed working with a lot more people than those who also became a friend outside of that environment.The other issue I’ve found is that these communities produce novel tools and ideas and AI can iterate on the idea much faster than the original authors. The original author had their own motivations for researching and producing and I can almost guarantee they weren’t reviewing the output of someone’s prompt.reply

title: OpenBSD 8.0 release will have inteldrm/radeondrm/amdgpu drivers from Linux 6.18 (bsd.network)
comments: OpenBSD 7.9 was already on the 6.18.y longterm support version for the drm(4) drivers, Jonathan Gray (jsg@) completed the update back in March, sponsored by the OpenBSD Foundation.https://marc.info/?l=openbsd-cvs&m=177310343311915&w=2I just wanted to highlight Jonathan's continued efforts backporting updates in my usual "HYPE" post series for the upcoming OpenBSD 8.0 release.(I'm the author of the mastodon post that was shared.)reply

Note that OpenBSD is on 7.9 now and all releases are possible breaking changes.They release every six month and increment by 0.1. And after 0.9 they rollover to the next whole number.So don’t think of version “8.0” as a major release per se, since OpenBSD is a fixed schedule release - not a Major.Minor release.reply

> OpenBSD is on 7.9 now and all releases are possible breaking changes.> don’t think of version “8.0” as a major release per se, since OpenBSD is a fixed schedule release - not a Major.Minor releaseAre these two statements a contradiction?Thinking out loud, maybe the spirit of your comment is, “Every OpenBSD release is possibly a breaking change; the version numbers don’t mean anything.”  Otherwise, I don’t see how it’s relevant to mention the current release ends in .9, then explain how the next version is constructed.Please help me understand.  I truly have no sense of how things work in OpenBSD land. The spirit of my comment here is entirely in good faith, just trying to learn.reply
What they meant is that, in terms of scale, the jump from 7.8 to 7.9 is more or less the same as the jump from 7.9 to 8.0This is similar to Linux kernel versioningreply

I think they mean in addition to all releases possibly having breaking changes, the developers did not pick 8.0 instead of 7.10 because they thought this is a significant milestone, but instead because they always roll from N.9 to (N+1).0.OpenBSD predates popular semantic versioning conventions by a few years.reply

nta but yes your spirit reading is correct. They're saying OpenBSD treats the version number as an integer, and every update adds .1. So 7.8 -> 7.9 -> 8.0, regardless of how significant or breaking the changes are.reply
How does GPL code get ported to BSD?reply

Most of the common drm code and kernel gpu drivers are already MIT/X licensed for historical reasons, same goes for the Mesa GL and Xorg components.https://github.com/openbsd/src/tree/master/sys/dev/pci/drmreply

Huh; I would have thought that importing MIT code into a GPL codebase (like the Linux kernel) essentially “beats out” the original MIT-licensing and instead creates an GPL-licensed fork of said code; thus making such forked code ineligible for re-import into an MIT/BSD-licensed project like the OpenBSD kernel (unless that project wants to be infected by the component’s licensing and become GPL-licensed in turn.)Are you saying instead that the DRM drivers in the Linux kernel (the in-tree parts, I mean, not the firmware blobs) exist as an island of MIT-licensed code inside the otherwise GPL-licensed codebase?Or are these parts of the Linux kernel not even technically in-tree, but rather developed in a separate canonical repo and frequently synchronized into the kernel as a vendored dependency? That’s the only way I can see this working; but it’s unclear to me why this state of things would have been maintained for any length of time when the Linux kernel was the only consumer…reply
No, you don't get to change the license on someone else's code just because you import it into your project.reply

comments: You don't actually have to do this - you can stick with a power of 2 sized table and just gently mix the hash value to get each additional bit index.(source - I wrote MurmurHash/SMHasher and have used the above in my own bloom filters and cuckoo hash tables)reply

Something like this? 64-bit hash, 9 bits to address all the bits in a 64-byte cache line, so 7 hash functions addressing the bits in a cache line can be extracted from a 64-bit hash?reply
yeah. You also don't need complete independence. You can use partially overlapping bits to get semi-independent hashes.reply

While much cheaper than going to disk, computing k independent hashes per key is still a bit expensive for very high performance systems.Depends how big the bloom filter is.  Most hashes are big and their bits are independent.reply

NB: You're trading non-negligible space efficiency here, which gets worse as you lower the false positive rate. Partitioning means uneven occupancy rates across partitions, and either you accept low occupancy (increased filter size overall) or you're pretty much guaranteed to have hot blocks (increased false positive rate for specific partitions).reply

You are describing "blocked" bloom filters here (i.e., the k hash functions are evaluated in a single block which is initially chosen by the hash). "Partitioned" bloom filters (i.e., each hash function is evaluated in a separate partition) don't have the imbalance problem you describe.reply

I'm describing the data structure from the article, which is partitioned twice: first into 64-byte, then into pairwise coprime-sized chunks. The 64-byte chunks are what you're quoting as "blocked", the pairwise coprime-sized chunks as "partitioned". The space inefficiency I mentioned applies to the 64-byte chunks.reply

first_paragraph: Note: as always, all my public writing is written by hand by me.A bloom filter is a probabilistic data structure that allows you to quickly and cheaply answer the question "is key X in this set?" with either "definitely not" or "probably".You pick a false positive rate that is acceptable for your workload and hardware, add keys to the set, and check for their existence later on.Bloom filters use a small amount of memory compared to the cardinality of the set, and are computationally very cheap. For these reasons, they're frequently used in high performance data systems.For example, a database might keep an in-memory bloom filter and check it before actually going to disk when looking up rows. This saves substantial amounts of very slow disk IO.We also use them all over the place in the Bluesky backend. In 2026, everything is a stream of numbers. It's obvious everything is a stream of numbers. We can save them to disk and stream them over the internet and archive them and it it were't for DRM and hostile practices we could stick them all in the same place right next to each other in the same directory.In let's say 1996, we weren't remotely there yet. A radio program was distinct from a television program was distinct from a book was distinct from a CD was distinct from a CD-ROM was distinct from a video game... and so on and so forth. You had a tool for recording from the TV, the VCR, but that didn't do the radio. You had a tool for that, which was a cassette tape, but that didn't do anything else. Except for certain early computers who took advantage of the fact that a cassette tape is really just a recording of varying voltages which can be fed into a computer to be interpreted as numbers, but this is one of the rare exceptions where there was some crossover, and by the 1990s this was gone anyhow. Now you had floppy disks, which were for computers, and they didn't store movies or books or radio shows, they just stored computer programs.Everything was compartmentalized so the idea of "storing a computer backup on a VHS tape" sounded like some sort of forbidden union.What sort of fascinates me about this history is how so much of it is written into the law now. We have all these different laws where music is treated this way, but movies are treated that way, and books are treated some other way, and so on and so forth. Copyright law isn't quite entirely broken up into unrelated fiefdoms but neither is it anywhere near as unified as it would be if it was a brand new idea someone was coming up with today. And it still has trouble dealing with the concept of things like "databases" sometimes.Now it's not such a weird idea that a VCR tape is really just a stream of numbers to be sliced and diced as needed for a project like this. But back then, so much of the processing involved fundementally analog processes that anything that crossed the streams seemed like magic. I don't feel like I've conveyed the idea properly that this wasn't just a technical thing, I'm talking about how people thought about these things. It was a revelation at the time that CDs could contain "video". It was a revelation that you could have "an MP3 player" that had "computer files", but, but, it played music. You could store backups on a CD. You could put a book... on a computer. I remember the first time I realized that if I took these cables from the VCR and fed them in to the input of my cassette player I could record the audio off a VCR on to a tape, the point being not that this was impossible but that it was something I had to realize. We had all these categories in our minds with strict boundaries between them that don't exist anymore, because those categories are just accidents of history.What we have today is much closer to reality... it's all just numbers. Any numbers can go on to number storage devices. Any numbers can be streamed across the number delivery service. The tech industry is in fact busily trying to re-establish the boundaries they themselves erased so they can artificially segment the various markets again.It's fun to see an old-school boundary breaker project again.reply
